                                 RESPONSE BRIEF OF VISTRA CORP.

           Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby submits this Response Brief pursuant to the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) December 18, 2025 Order in Docket No. EL25-49 et

al. (“Order on Show Cause Proceeding” or “Order”),1 and its Notice of Extension of Time,2 in the

 above-captioned dockets. The Commission’s landmark Order articulated a vision for providing

service to large loads that are co-located with generation resources in the PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C. (“PJM”) region in order to fulfill customers’ “right to receive electric service on a timely

basis” while ensuring that service is “reliable and affordable for all customers.”3 To do that, the

Commission required a replacement rate that ensures that large loads are “able to take transmission

services that reflect their actual impact on the transmission system.”4 Critically, the Commission

directed PJM to create new transmission services to facilitate the expeditious development and

interconnection of new loads co-located with generation resources in PJM.5 Such co-location will

be critical to powering the next generation of digital infrastructure necessary to develop and

maintain the artificial intelligence (“AI”) capability that is increasingly central to our national

security.

         But as is often the case, the devil is in the details. While the Commission set forth the

overarching framework for the new services, the actual rates, terms, and conditions will be

developed in this paper hearing. Those details will determine whether or not these new services

accomplish the goals the Commission articulated. Unfortunately, the details proposed by PJM and

To adopt a replacement rate that is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory, and to ensure

that the new transmission services actually meet the needs they were created to fulfill, the

Commission must direct PJM and the Transmission Owners to remedy various flaws in the

proposal. As discussed further below, although there are numerous flaws in PJM and the

Transmission Owners’ proposal, they can be grouped into three categories.

         First, PJM proposes to delay the effectiveness of the new transmission services until June

1, 2029. Under that proposal, customers may have to wait until June 1, 2029 to even submit study

requests associated with the new transmission services. In effect, that proposal creates a three- to

five-year moratorium on the co-location of new large loads and generation in PJM—quite the

opposite of “break[ing] the logjam.”6

         Second, the proposed rates, terms, and conditions for Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service are both unreasonable and unduly discriminatory. While the Commission

compared Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service to Non-Firm Point-to-Point

Transmission Service,7 PJM and the Transmission Owners propose to make Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service both more expensive and less available than its point-to-point

counterpart.

         Third, the proposal reserves unfettered discretion for PJM and the Transmission Owners in

the study process. The proposal appears to allow PJM and the Transmission Owners to determine,

for each transmission service request, whether studies are required, which studies to conduct, the

textbook opportunities for the type of undue discrimination that the Order was intended to prevent.

       The Commission must direct PJM and the Transmission Owners to address each of these

items on further compliance to render the PJM Tariff just, reasonable, and not unduly

discriminatory. The Commission can do so through the below targeted adjustments to PJM and

the Transmission Owners’ proposal. In directing further compliance, Vistra urges the Commission

to provide as specific and detailed guidance as possible, in addition to setting tight compliance

deadlines, to achieve the Commission’s laudable goal of providing the clarity needed to promote

the expeditious interconnection of large loads.

   Facilitate speed to power by requiring PJM to implement the new transmission services sooner,
    with a transition process that reflects the services that can be provided most quickly and
    respects ongoing or completed necessary studies.
   Ensure that the rate structure for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service is tailored
    to the benefits that the customer draws from the grid and does not create cost shifts.
       o The rates for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service should recognize that
         customers may use the service differently, i.e., some customers may never reserve
         transmission service, some may reserve a de minimis amount, and some may reserve
         significant amounts. Those customers do not rely on the grid to the same extent and
         should not be subject to the same grid reliance charge.
   Eliminate unfettered discretion in the proposed study process by ensuring that the Tariff clearly
    defines the studies that must occur and the timeline and order in which those studies will occur.
   Remove unreasonable and unduly discriminatory restrictions on the use of special protective
    schemes and remedial action schemes. Any restrictions must comply with comparability
    principles and be governed by clear and objective standards to prevent undue discrimination.

I. The Proposed June 1, 2029 Effective Date is Unjust and Unreasonable and Fails to
   Provide Speed to Power

       This entire proceeding exists because co-located loads need to access the transmission

system quickly in order to satisfy the nation’s time-sensitive demand for the computing and




                                                  -5-
 manufacturing capability necessary to win the global race for AI dominance.8 As Commissioner

Rosner put it, “a business-as-usual approach to load growth . . . will not suffice to timely meet

growing demand while also keeping prices reasonable.”9 Indeed, the new transmission services

created in this proceeding were created specifically “to facilitate more rapid interconnection and

operation of Co-Located Loads[.]”10

         PJM nevertheless proposes to delay the implementation of the new transmission services

until June 1, 2029—nearly four years after the Commission’s directive to take action.11 And

customers may not even be able to submit study requests until the tariff provisions governing those

applications are effective. A June 1, 2029 effective date means, then, that co-located loads will

not begin to receive service in PJM until 2030 at the earliest—and potentially even later, depending

on the length of PJM’s studies and the scope of required network upgrades.

          PJM has not shown that its four-year delay is just and reasonable.12 Nor can it. PJM

presents two arguments in support of its four-year delay: (1) the need to procure capacity to serve

new load through the three-year forward schedule of the capacity market, and (2) the need for

software updates to PJM’s market and operations systems to permit the curtailment of Non-Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service and Interim Network Integration Transmission Service

(“NITS”) when needed.13 Neither bears scrutiny.

    A. Capacity Market

         PJM’s capacity market schedule does not justify delaying the provision of new

transmission services. As a threshold matter, resource adequacy considerations are simply outside

the scope of a transmission provider’s obligation to serve: the Commission requires transmission

providers to make transmission service decisions based on available transfer capacity.14 Moreover,

two out of the three new transmission services are non-firm. PJM does not need to procure capacity

    C. The Commission Should Require a Transition Process that Accommodates Co-

        Even if the Commission accepts PJM’s unsupported assertion that it will take a third of a

decade to update its software, the Commission should require PJM to immediately accommodate

co-location arrangements for which those software changes are, as a practical matter, irrelevant.

transmission service to the extent that the Eligible Customer will not withdraw any electricity from

the transmission system.”32 In that case, the customer will simply be charged for regulation and

black start services.33
